content.summary_of_the_paper: The proposed GOAT is formulated via (1) Pre-train the node embeddings as our positional embeddings via Node2Vec. (2) Adopt an EMA k-means algorithm to generate k centroids in the graph and the corresponding hidden embeddings; then, the embeddings of the centroids are used as the key and value matrices in the scalable global attention. Theoretical justifications are provided to reveal the error bounds between the proposed scalable global attention and the traditional self-attention. (3) Introduce a local attention module in the form of message-passing that focuses on each node's local neighborhood. The authors show that GOAT can scale to large-scale graphs and is generally competitive in different dataset settings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

- The proposed scalable global attention reduces the time complexity of the self-attention to $O(nk)$, making it feasible to generalize to large-scale graphs.
- Theoretical justifications reveal the error bounds between the proposed scalable global attention and the traditional self-attention.

## Weaknesses

### Majors

The novelty of this work seems limited to the direct utilization of existing methods.

- Scalable Global Attention: The EMA $k$-Means method is used to generate $k$ centroids in the graph and the corresponding hidden embeddings; then, the embeddings of the centroids are utilized as the key and value matrices. The EMA and the $k$-means algorithm are existing methods, and simply combining them to ‘coarsen’ the input graph seems to lack novelty.
- Local Attention: GAT performs the masked attention by only calculating the attention between central node $v_i$ and its neighborhood $\mathcal N_{i}$ [1]. By setting the $\mathcal N_i$ as the $k$-hop neighborhood of $v_i$, the Local Attention seems very similar to a GAT, with minor differences in GAT’s simplified attention and Local Attention’s self-attention.

The $k$-means algorithm suffers from several problems [2] like (1) being sensitive to initialization, (2) performance degradation when the data is not well described by reasonably separated spherical balls, (3) sensitive to the presence of outliers, (4) the pre-defined $k$, and so on. As a major essence of GOAT, these vulnerabilities of the $k$-means algorithms should be analyzed, if not theoretically, at least empirically.

The authors claimed that "the local attention module provides increased capacity to learn the inductive biases required for accurate predictions beyond the hardcoded structures of existing GNNs." However, such a claim is not well supported by either discussions or experiments, and I think simply categorizing GNNs into "a recursive 1-hop neighbor smoothing pattern" is not quite correct. Also, in the code provided, the local attention is implemented by GNN's message-passing. I wonder what exact differences separate the local attention from the GNNs, or it's simply a form of GNNs? More analysis and discussions may be provided, and an experiment replacing the local attention module with certain GNNs may also help demonstrate the design's effeciveness.

The experiments conducted by the authors seem not very promising.

- Almost all GNNs baselines are early-stage models. The newest model LINKX was proposed in 2021, and other GNN baselines were proposed in 2017, 2018, and 2019. Regarding homophily and heterophily data mining, there are brunches of newly proposed models that can be considered in the comparison. Although some of the methods suffer from scalability issues, there are a series of small or medium-sized graphs that are widely adopted in the domain of homophily and heterophily data mining, like Cora, Texas, and Chameleon [3]. These datasets may be adopted, too. The current comparison seems incomplete and limited.
- No Graph Transformer baselines are involved. I understand that it can be computationally infeasible to compute some Graph Transformer methods, but I think it would then be worthwhile to include a few datasets that other Graph Transformer methods have been developed on, e.g., PATTERN/CLUSTER (so as to be able to use the results from their papers), and they are also large-scale datasets designed for the node-classification tasks. Further, small or medium-sized graphs like Cora, Texas, and Chameleon [3] can be considered. I think it is beneficial that this paper considers varied datasets, and I do not imply that the authors should instead use datasets other authors have used. Rather, the last years have seen explosive growth in the research domain of Graph Transformers, so the current comparison seems incomplete/limited if none of them are included in the experiments. A full comparison involving concurrent GNNs and Graph Transformers on these datasets may further investigate the abilities of GOAT.
- For the arXiv-year, there exist official public splits shared by [3], and I noticed that the model LINKX proposed by [3] is also used as a baseline. I encourage the authors to run the models on public splits instead of random splits. This would help gauge the benefits of hetero/homophilic settings on the standard benchmark.

### Minors

Several related works are missing. Transformers with fast attention (like [4,5]) seem to be related to GOAT, as they approximate self-attention in linear time and are compatible with absolute PEs. I encourage the authors to supplement the corresponding details.

The time complexity of the traditional self-attention in Transformer is $O(n^2d)$, not the claimed $O(n^2)$.

### Questions

Q1. As claimed by the authors, scalable local attention is the approximation of global self-attention with error bounds. Then how does GOAT compare to linear Transformers (which also approximate the self-attention) like [4,5], with the pertained node embeddings via Node2Vec or some GNNs as PEs?

Q2. What is the efficiency of performing the EMA K-Means algorithm? As claimed by the authors, the EMA K-Means algorithm should be run on the fly during the training process. I would be interested to know the actual runtime and also the parameter number of GOAT compared to the baselines.


[1] Veličković, Petar, et al. "Graph attention networks." ICLR 2018

[2] Wu, Xindong, et al. "Top 10 algorithms in data mining." *Knowledge and information systems*
 14.1 (2008): 1-37.

[3] Lim, Derek, et al. "Large scale learning on non-homophilous graphs: New benchmarks and strong simple methods." NeurIPS 2021.

[4] Kitaev, Nikita, Łukasz Kaiser, and Anselm Levskaya. "Reformer: The efficient transformer." ICLR 2020.

[5] Liutkus, Antoine, et al. "Relative positional encoding for transformers with linear complexity." **ICML 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity and reproducibility of this paper are relatively good, although Figure 1 in the paper confuses me during the reading. While Neighborhood Sampling is not the essence of GOAT, why does it consume most places with irrelevant details, leaving the core modules unelaborated?

For quality and novelty, I think there is much to be improved. Please refer to the “Strengths & Weaknesses” section.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed GOAT generalizes the Transformer architecture to large-scale graph representation learning, while there exist major weaknesses, including lack of novelty, missing discussion on core modules, unsupported claims, and insufficient experiments.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes GOAT, a Transformer-based model for node-level tasks over large-scale graphs. To reduce the intractable quadratic complexity of naïve transformer, this work proposes to use dimensional reduction strategy such that each node only need to attend to the nodes in the codebook obtained by the dimensional reduction. Experiments on both homophilous and heterophilous graphs have been conducted to evaluate the proposed approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
#####Strength#####

1. The usage of the codebook is novel. With the K-means based reduction method, the complexity of the global attention can be reduced significantly. 

2. The empirical results are good on both homophilous and heterophilous graphs, which can support the effectiveness of the proposed model.

3. This manuscript is clearly written and easy to follow.

#####Weaknesses#####

1. The local module is not new, since it is the same as the widely used neighbor sampling technique. Having said that, the main novel part of this approach is the proposed dimensional reduction idea for global attention. However, more justifications of this part are still missing. (1) It is unclear why it is necessary to use positional encoding and why we use node2vec for the global module. (2) In this work, there is a cluster-based attention bias term to adjust the attention scores for global attention. It is unclear how this bias term affects the attention. Maybe it would be more convincing to visualize the learned attention scores. Otherwise, it is unclear how the proposed global module compares to the model where we just aggregate features from each node’s corresponding centroid.

2. Since the key contribution of this work is the dimensional reduction idea for global attention, I think more empirical analysis of this component should be provided. For example, a visualization of the global attention scores or the obtained K-means centroids would provide deeper understanding of the approach.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think this work has merits in terms of the methodology part. However, I believe deeper analysis of the key components should be given to make it into a strong submission.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a scalable graph transformer called GOAT. Instead of computing the attention weights of all node pairs, GOAT firstly conducts the k-means algorithm to divide all nodes into several clusters, then calculates the attention value between the target node and the centroid of each cluster to obtain the approximate global attention. GOAT also develops a local attention module to capture the rich local information of graphs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This paper develops a k-means based strategy for approximately calculating the attention weights of all nodes, which reduces the computational cost of the self-attention module.
- The authors provide the theoretical support for the proposed method.
Weaknesses:
- Since the k-means algorithm is utilized for clustering, the value of k is important for the model performance. However, there is no discussion on the setting of k in this paper. Intuitively, graphs with different sizes may require different values of k. Unfortunately, the analysis of k on different graphs is missing in the experiments. 
- This paper lacks the complexity analysis of the whole training process since the training stage involves extra operations compared to the original Transformer, such as clustering and node sampling.
- I am confused by line 6 of Algorithm 1 about the calculation of matrix V. Q and K are determined by the features of attribute information and structural information. However, V is only derived from the attribute features. The reason for this difference is missing in this paper.
- How does the local attention module generate the node representations? And how does GOAT utilize global and local attention to learn the final representations of nodes? Besides, the ablation study for comparing the performance of global attention and local attention is missing. I am curious about the performance of GOAT with only global attention since the structural information is absorbed in the global attention module.
- Many powerful methods are not considered as baselines, such as GCNII[1] and GloGNN[2], which makes the experimental results not very convincing. Since authors utilize the sampling method to generalize the full-batch GNNs to large graphs. Therefore, some powerful full-batch GNNs[1][3][4] should be considered as baselines.
Besides, the author should consider comparing the effectiveness of GOAT with advanced scalable GNNs, such as GBP[5] and GRAND+[6].
In addition, the experiments are only based on four datasets (actually three), which is not enough to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Widely used datasets in this community, such as datasets in the recent work [2] for node classification on homophilous and heterophilous graphs, should be added to the experiments.
- The authors have a wrong understanding of GNN for heterophilous graphs. Actually, recent advanced GNNs [2][4][7] for heterophilous graphs also obtain powerful performance on homophilous graphs. However, the authors think that heterophily-centered GNNs do not work for homophilous graphs. Therefore, I suggest that the authors carefully review the recent works and reorganize the introduction and related work of this paper.

[1] Chen M, et al. Simple and Deep Graph Convolutional Networks. ICML, 2020.
[2] Li X, et al. Finding Global Homophily in Graph Neural Networks When Meeting Heterophily. ICML, 2022.
[3] Klicpera J, et al. Predict then Propagate: Graph Neural Networks Meet Personalized Pagerank. ICLR, 2019.
[4] Chien E, et al. Adaptive Universal Generalized Pagerank Graph Neural Network. ICLR, 2021.
[5] Chen M, et al. Scalable Graph Neural Networks via Bidirectional Propagation. NeurIPS, 2020.
[6] Feng W, et al. GRAND+: Scalable Graph Random Neural Networks. WWW, 2022.
[7] He D, et al. Block Modeling-guided Graph Convolutional Neural Networks. AAAI, 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing is not very clear, and some opinions are wrong. 
The proposed method has the theoretical support. But the inadequate experimental results can’t convince the effectiveness of the proposed method.
This paper proposes a reasonably novel idea for reducing the training cost of graph transformers.
content.summary_of_the_review: The analysis is not enough, the experiments are inadequate, and some claims look wrong. The overall writing needs to be improved to make all details clear.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
